messages.subject: Weird results with nbinomial regression
parts:
Hi everyone. I have one question regarding a negative binomial regression with a random error in the linear predictor. This is the setup:

library(INLA)
#> This is INLA_20.03.09 built 2020-03-09 09:12:35 UTC.

set.seed(20042020)
n <- 544
ID <- 1:n
x <- rnorm(n)
random_error <- rnorm(n)
eta <- 1 + x + random_error
E <- runif(n, 0, 1)
mu <- E * exp(eta)

size <- 3
y <- rnbinom(n, size = size, mu = mu)

I choose n = 544 since the objective was simulating a spatial besag error following the instructions here and, in that case, g$n = 544. This is the summary of the estimation:

summary(inla(
  formula = y ~ x + f(ID),
  family = "nbinomial",
  data = list(y = y, x = x, ID = ID, E = E),
  control.inla = list(strategy = "laplace"),
  verbose = FALSE,
  E = E
))
#>
#> Call:
#>    c("inla(formula = y ~ x + f(ID), family = \"nbinomial\", data = list(y
#>    = y, ", " x = x, ID = ID, E = E), E = E, verbose = FALSE, control.inla
#>    = list(strategy = \"laplace\"))" )
#> Time used:
#>     Pre = 2.59, Running = 26.9, Post = 0.301, Total = 29.8
#> Fixed effects:
#>                   mean        sd    0.025quant    0.5quant     0.975quant         mode          kld
#> (Intercept) 0.776    0.075             0.642         0.772              0.932        0.762      0.005
#> x                1.118    0.078             0.967         1.117              1.272        1.116      0.000
#>
#> Random effects:
#>   Name     Model
#>     ID IID model
#>
#> Model hyperparameters:
#>                                                                                              mean               sd     0.025quant  0.5quant  0.975quant       mode
#> size for the nbinomial observations (1/overdispersion)   2.43e+04   7.59e+06            18.279     247.23     6.80e+04    27.945
#> Precision for ID                                                                 7.28e-01    1.14e-01              0.486        0.74       9.08e-01      0.796
#>
#> Expected number of effective parameters(stdev): 274.81(14.30)
#> Number of equivalent replicates : 1.98
#>
#> Marginal log-Likelihood:  -959.79

The results are quite strange but the weirdest part is that if I repeat the same simulation with n = 500 then everything seems to work fine.

set.seed(20042020)
n <- 500
ID <- 1:n
x <- rnorm(n)
random_error <- rnorm(n)
eta <- 1 + x + random_error
E <- runif(n, 0, 1)
mu <- E * exp(eta)

size <- 3
y <- rnbinom(n, size = size, mu = mu)

summary(inla(
  formula = y ~ x + f(ID),
  family = "nbinomial",
  data = list(y = y, x = x, ID = ID, E = E),
  control.inla = list(strategy = "laplace"),
  verbose = FALSE,
  E = E
))
#>
#> Call:
#>    c("inla(formula = y ~ x + f(ID), family = \"nbinomial\", data = list(y
#>    = y, ", " x = x, ID = ID, E = E), E = E, verbose = FALSE, control.inla
#>    = list(strategy = \"laplace\"))" )
#> Time used:
#>     Pre = 1.61, Running = 25.1, Post = 0.284, Total = 27
#> Fixed effects:
#>                         mean            sd      0.025quant      0.5quant     0.975quant       mode      kld
#> (Intercept)        1.139       0.140               0.873           1.144              1.394       1.183        0
#> x                       1.007       0.076              0.860            1.006             1.156        1.005       0
#>
#> Random effects:
#>   Name     Model
#>     ID IID model
#>
#> Model hyperparameters:
#>                                                                                              mean             sd      0.025quant 0.5quant 0.975quant     mode
#> size for the nbinomial observations (1/overdispersion)          1.33        0.377               0.768        1.27            2.24      1.16
#> Precision for ID                                                                       1.91       0.668                0.881       1.82             3.48      1.64
#>
#> Expected number of effective parameters(stdev): 131.03(49.66)
#> Number of equivalent replicates : 3.82
#>
#> Marginal log-Likelihood:  -909.06

I'm sorry if this is a dumb question, but what's the problem here? Did I code something wrong in setting up the simulations? I also include a complete reprex of the problem here.

As always thank you very much for your help.
Andrea Gilardi

messages.author: 3eab71733027a24a
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Weird results with nbinomial regression
parts:
Hi,

I'm not quite sure what exactly is 'weird', I am not surprised about
the results.

The negative binomial can be reinterpreted as poisson regression with
an added (independent) random effect

y ~ 1 + ... + u

where u_i is loggamma distributed, and if you integrated u_i out,
you'll get the nbinomial.

adding another (indep) random effect, like

y ~ 1 + ... + u + v

then, with single observation, you only observe one observation for
each u_i+v_i, so only the prior (essentially) determine what is 'u' and
what is 'v', since only their sum is likelihood identifiable.

with replication, your size 3, then j=1..3, so you observe

u_i1 + v_i
u_i2 + v_i
u_i3 + v_i

which means that identfication of what is 'u' and what is 'v' is now
much much easier.

H

Hi and thanks for your reply.

The thing that surprised me most (and that I think is weird) is the fact that creating two almost identical simulations with slightly different n (544 vs 500) resulted in totally different results. Is this due only to randomness? When I repeat the same simulations with other values of n (100, 200, 1000) I get again totally different results. Does it mean that it's not possible to estimate separately the size effect and the random effect?

The negative binomial can be reinterpreted as poisson regression with
an added (independent) random effect

        y ~ 1 + ... + u

where u_i is loggamma distributed, and if you integrated u_i out,
you'll get the nbinomial.

adding another (indep) random effect, like

        y ~ 1 + ... + u + v

then, with single observation, you only observe one observation for
each u_i+v_i, so only the prior (essentially) determine what is 'u' and
what is 'v', since only their sum is likelihood identifiable.
Ok and it makes sense. But the priors in the two examples are the same, right? Moreover, I'm sorry if this should be obvious, but I don't understand the following sentences:

with replication, your size 3, then j=1..3, so you observe

        u_i1 + v_i
        u_i2 + v_i
        u_i3 + v_i

What do you mean by u_i1, u_i2 and u_i3 in the previous example?

Kind regards
Andrea
